$comment: Receptor modalities and the physics that decides which of them a given planet can evolve. Every band carries the numbers the viability test needs; nothing here is switched on by name.

constants.$why_photoisomerisation: 11-cis retinal isomerises at about 1.5 eV. Below that no pigment-based photoreceptor can work at all, whatever the animal wants, because the photon cannot do the chemistry.

bands.why: Ionising. A detector is a damage counter, not an eye. Only worth anything on a world with a real radiation flux — which is exactly where radiotrophy shows up too.
Sterilising. Reaches the ground only without ozone, and a receptor here is a warning organ.
Bee-visible band. Present on any world with a hot star and a thin ozone column.
Penetrates seawater furthest — which is why deep-sea eyes converge on 480 nm on Earth and why a deep ocean anywhere selects this band.
Peak of a G-star's photon flux at the ground. The default only because the star is the default.
Chlorophyll's red edge sits at the top of this band, so a red-sensitive eye is also a life-detector.
Where an M dwarf actually puts its photons — Wien peak for 3000 K is 966 nm. On a red-dwarf world this is the visible band, and a pigment can still just about do the chemistry down to about 1000 nm.

Thermal. A photon here carries roughly 0.1 eV, far too little to isomerise a pigment, so this is a heat-difference organ — a pit, not an eye — and it is swamped by the animal's own emission unless the aperture is cold or the sensor is differential. Two millikelvin is about the floor a pit organ reaches.
Blocked by water vapour on any wet world. Useful only on a dry, cold, thin-atmosphere planet.

A 1 mm photon is 1.24 meV — about 0.05 kT at 300 K, so no chemical receptor can ever register one. Microwave sight is therefore an antenna or a cooled bolometer, and the diffraction limit is brutal: 1.22 lambda over D at 1 mm needs a four-metre aperture to match a human eye. Which means microwave eyes are not impossible, they are a body-size problem — and a cold, large, radio-quiet world is where they get paid for.
Non-imaging at any plausible aperture. Useful for signalling and for sensing a magnetosphere, not for seeing.

Needs a conducting medium. In seawater a muscle twitch is a microvolt-per-centimetre field at a metre; in air it is nothing. Evolved independently at least eight times on Earth, always in water, and it is the correct answer for a lightless subsurface ocean.
Only worth having where there is a field to sense, so a world with no dynamo has no magnetoreception and no long-distance migration built on it.

Resolution scales with frequency and with the speed of sound in the medium, so a dense hot atmosphere is a better ear than a thin cold one. Echolocation is imaging by this route and it is what you get when the photon budget is zero.
The oldest sense and the only one available to a cell. Gradient-following in a fluid; range set by diffusion and by advection, so a windy or a current-swept world smells further.
Near-field flow imaging. Free to a body that already has a surface in a fluid, and it works in total darkness at short range.
Ambient temperature, not radiated. Available to anything with a membrane.
Which way is down. A dense grain in a hair-lined sac — the cheapest organ in this table, and it does not work in free fall or on a body in orbit.
Sky polarisation gives a compass under overcast, and underwater it gives contrast against transparent prey. Requires an ordered receptor array, so it comes with an imaging eye or not at all.

$utilityNote: How much of a life a body can run on this sense alone, once it is receiving it. An imaging photon band is 1.0; a gravity sense tells you one thing. provenance: fitted — it is the ranking that decides which sense a lineage invests in, and it is the one number in this file that is a judgement rather than a measurement.
